headline: The Thanksgiving when actual elephants marched down Broadway
author: Maegan Vazquez

paragraphs.text: In 1924, to celebrate the expansion of its Herald Square department store — and to promote the start of the Christmas shopping season — Macy’s invited the public to a Thanksgiving Day parade through Manhattan. Costumed company employees were joined by live Central Park Zoo animals, elephants included, for the 6-mile jaunt down Broadway from Harlem to Herald Square.
Plans included a cage match between grizzly bears. For the finale, Santa Claus climbed atop Macy’s new 34th Street marquee to show off the store’s holiday displays.
The parade would become an annual tradition. Zoo animals would soon be retired, and it would be christened the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1934.
Santa Claus has closed the event nearly every year since, but many traditions now synonymous with it began years or decades after its inception.

It would be a few years before the first giant balloon, the street-smart cartoon character Felix the Cat, made its debut. The event was aired on NBC radio in 1932 and in an experimental shortwave telecast in 1939. CBS broadcast segments from the parade in 1948. NBC, its current home, began broadcasting to a national audience in 1952, according to Macy’s.
The Radio City Rockettes kicked off their first parade performance in 1958. The Tom Turkey float was introduced in 1973. And Broadway performances were added in 1980.
The Thanksgiving Day storm that lashed the East Coast on Thursday led organizers to move this year’s parade to Saturday. It was the first postponement, but not the first time adjustments were needed.
The event was called on account of World War II from 1942 through 1944. A helium shortage in 1958 led organizers to use cranes to hold aloft giant balloons filled with ordinary air.
High winds grounded balloons in 1971. In 1997, a Cat in the Hat balloon hit a lamppost, knocking loose debris that sent a woman into a 24-day coma and injured three other people.
During the coronavirus pandemic, the 2020 production was shrunk to a single block, closed to the public and videotaped over multiple days.
The 100th edition of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade kicks off at 8:30 a.m. Eastern time Saturday.
Photo Almanac is an occasional series from The Washington Post, using photo archives to examine where we’ve been to understand where we are.
